# Seafaring

*Pages PDF 103-120*

## **Seafaring Handling a Boat Upon the Seas and Navigating Ocean Hazards**
**Sea of Claws** presents several different sets of rules for vessels, depending on different circumstances. These rules are broken down as follows. 

If the boat is being propelled by sail, the Boat Handling Test is made using the Sail Skill of the Character who is guiding the tiller. 

**Seafaring** (this chapter) gives the basic rules for making progress, manoeuvring, navigating, and fighting on a boat. The rules are intended to be used for small vessels making short journeys, where the Characters on board a ship outnumber the NPCs. In other words, if the party want to take their barge out for a brief sojourn upon the waves, this chapter has all they may need. 

**Sailing Larger Vessels** (page 121) gives advice on what it is like to manage a craft where the actions of individuals matter less than the coordination of a large crew. In situations where named Characters are in the minority, such as if they join the crew of an Imperial warship for a scenario, use these rules. 

**Longer Voyages** (page 128) provides a version of the Endeavours rules from **WFRP** to account for lengthy journeys at sea. In situations where a GM must account for an epic voyage, but wants to reach the destination without having to give daily updates, use these rules. 

## **Small Boats on the Ocean**
If the boat is being propelled by oars, the Boat Handling Test is made using the Row Skill of the rower with the highest Row Skill (other rowers may assist). 

- Characters with the Lore (Oceans) Skill may take a bonus to Boat Handling Tests equal to the first digit of their Skill score — for example, a character with a Lore (Oceans) Skill of 36 would receive a bonus of +3 to Boat Handling Tests. This bonus applies only while on the ocean. 

## **The Character at the Tiller**
Often when describing the need to take a Boat Handling Test the rules will mention the Character at the Tiller. This refers to whichever Character is best placed to influence effective movement of the vessel at the time of the Test. They may receive assistance from other Characters as explained on **WFRP** , page 155. The Character at the Tiller need not be at an actual tiller, they may be at the wheel, the sails, rowing the boat, or in any position from which they can determine the boat’s direction. 

Boat Handling rules were introduced into Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay in the **Death on the Reik Companion** , and small river-going boats are also used on the ocean. The bays and estuaries of the northern Empire play host to many fishing boats and visits from small trading barges. These boats are like the boats described for river travel in their appearance and operation. For fuller explanations of these rules, refer to the **Death on the Reik Companion** , though note that the rules here are less forgiving in that Characters without the Sail Skill are unable to pilot a sailing vessel on the ocean, and that Skill Tests are required to make progress. 

- ‘Boat Handling Tests’ is a generic name for the Skill Tests needed to ensure a boat makes progress and performs manoeuvres appropriately. 

## Other Forms of Propulsion
**Sea of Claws** mostly deals with boats crewed by the sailors of the Empire or the marauders of the Norse tribes. These seafarers rely on oars or sails to propel their vessels. There are other seafarers in the world, however, who make use of other forms of propulsion.

Like Characters, boats have a Movement Attribute that determines their average speed. Movement Characteristics and their approximate speeds are listed below.

Shifts are approximate times related to how tiring it is to work with sails or oars. **Example:** _Andreas is the Character at the tiller of a skiff. He has someone else on board to help him trim the sails, and so the ship has the minimum crew needed to use its Sail M of 3._ 

_Andreas has a Sail skill of 53 with which to make Boat Handling Tests. Conditions are a little rough, but no obstacles present themselves, so the GM decides he can make a single_ _**Challenging (+0) Boat Handling** Test to cover a whole eight hour shift. Andreas scores 41, a success with +1 SL._ 

_The skiff counts as having M of 4 due to the +1 SL,  and therefore covers 24 miles before the next test is required._ 

## **Pushing It**
A crew can attempt to increase their vessel’s speed, either by making efforts to catch the wind in the best way possible, or by rowing harder. There is a limit to how much faster a boat can go, and to benefit from the movement bonus, a Sail or Row Test must be passed as explained in the table below. **Note:** this is not a Boat Handling Test and Lore (Oceans) does not provide a benefit. 

||**PUSHING IT**<br>**M Bonus**<br>**Sail**<br>**Oars**<br>+1<br>Very Hard<br>(–30) Sail Test<br>Hard (–20) Row Test<br>+2<br>n/a<br>Very Hard (–30) Row Test|
|---|---|

The Movement Bonus lasts until the next shift (8 hours for sailing, 2 for rowing) or until circumstances call for another Boat Handling Test. 

## **Exhaustion**
Operating a vessel is hard work. At the end of a shift, crew involved in Sailing or Rowing must make an **Average (+20) Endurance** Test or receive a _Fatigued_ Condition. If these crewmembers have been Pushing It (see above), this becomes a **Difficult (–10) Endurance** Test. 

## **Manoeuvres**
Ships may need to make intricate manoeuvres in order to avoid obstacles or bring their guns to bear on an enemy. 

## **Manoeuvre Tests**
Whenever a manoeuvre is called for, the Character at the tiller makes a Manoeuvre Test. This is a Boat Handling Test modified by the Man Characteristic of the boat, as well as other factors the GM finds pertinent. Manoeuvre Tests are a type of Boat Handling Test, and any factors that apply to Boat Handling Tests also apply to Manoeuvre Tests, though factors noted as applying to Manoeuvre Tests do not benefit Boat Handling Tests made for other purposes. 

## Maximum Speeds
There are several ways in which a vessel can improve its speed, but exceeding the speeds for which it was designed subjects a boat to forces that may damage it. 

A boat may move at a rate up to M+4 without the risk of taking damage. A boat moving at a faster rate must succeed at a Toughness Test or suffer Damage according to the **She Cannot Take it, Skipper!** table.

## **Fouling**
Over time a boat that remains on the ocean will begin to accrue a layer of seaweed and barnacles on its hull, as well as shipworm and boring beetles within its timbers. The reliability of a vessel is compromised by such infestation. 

Every week that a ship is out at sea without appropriate maintenance, make a Toughness Test for the vessel. Each failed Test adds a level of Fouling. This has the effects described in the Fouling table. 

Fouling can be removed from smaller vessels through creative use of Skills, Spells, or Miracles, or even by beaching the boat and applying some elbow grease. To clean a boat of Average Size or larger, it would need to be taken to a dedicated dock to be scraped.

## **Weather**
Weather on the Sea of Claws is famously changeable. The Sea of Claws Weather table gives the day’s weather in relation to Precipitation, Winds, Visibility, and Temperature. Roll for each aspect. If you get a series of results that feels unearthly, this could either be put down to the Winds of Magic streaming from the Chaos Wastes to the north, or you may decide to roll again. The base scores are for the summer, so you should add 2 to the result for the spring and autumn months, and 4 for winter. 

## **Temperature**
High or low temperatures can have pronounced effects 

on the performance of a crew. 

## **Sweltering**
Every two hours, make a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** Test. If the Test is failed, suffer the effects of Heat Exposure as explained on **WFRP** , page 181. Crew members must drink two gallons of water a day or else **WFRP** , page 181. suffer from Thirst, as explained on 

## **Hot**
The table is designed to represent weather on the Sea of Claws. On warmer seas subtract 2 from rolls for Temperature and Visibility. 

Every four hours, make an **Average (+20) Endurance** Test. If the Test is failed, suffer the effects of Heat Exposure. Crew members must drink two gallons of water a day or else suffer from Thirst.

Moderately cool or warm, the temperature is tolerable and has no effect on the crew. 

## **Chilly**
Every four hours, make an **Average (+20) Endurance** Test. If the Test is failed, suffer the effects of Cold Exposure as explained on **WFRP** , page 181. 

## **Bitter**
Every two hours, make a **Challenging (+0) Endurance** 

Test. If the Test is failed, suffer effects of Cold Exposure.

## **Winds**
The aspect of the weather which affects sailing most seriously is the wind, but it has a much greater impact on sea travel than it does on river vessels. Roll on the following table to randomly determine the direction of the wind. 

||**D10 roll**<br>**Wind Direction**<br>1–6<br>Prevailing (on the Sea of Claws the prevailing<br>winds are westerlies, the GM may decide the<br>direction ofprevailingwinds on other oceans).<br>7<br>Northerly<br>8<br>Southerly<br>9<br>Westerly<br>10<br>Easterly|

To see what impact the wind has on the ship you must determine which direction the wind is blowing and compare that to the direction the ship is attempting to travel. For clarity: a northerly wind blows from the north, starboard is to the left of the ship (from the perspective of someone facing the same direction as the ship), and port to the right.

## **Becalmed**
The boat may not move under sail. Unless it has a backup method of propulsion the boat either remains in place or is pulled along in the direction of the current (currents vary in strength, but most pull ships along at a Movement rate of 1; tidal currents or those leading to a whirlpool pull ships along at faster rates, see pages 112 and 113). 

If the vessel possesses a Ship’s Boat that is equipped with oars, this may be deployed to tug the larger vessel along. If this process is followed, the two boats move together as if they were a single craft with M1, suffering –3 SL to its Man Characteristic. 

## **Tack**
A movement increase can be achieved by tacking, which requires a successful **Challenging (+0) Boat Handling** Test. If this Test is failed, the boat moves as normal, with no bonus. 

## **Batten Down**
Roll on the Sea of Claws Weather table at the start of a journey to determine the strength of the wind; thereafter, check at dawn, midday, dusk, and midnight by rolling d10 and consulting the Wind Effect table; a result of 1 indicates that the wind has changed by one step, with an equal chance of becoming stronger or lighter. The Doldrums can only change to Light Breeze, and Violent Storm winds can only change to a Strong Gale. 

Numbers shown impact the speed of a vessel. These numbers should be added to the boat’s M or the distances travelled before any other modifiers are applied. Numbers before the slash indicate the effect on a ship propelled by sails, and the number after the slash to vessels powered by other means. 

Strong winds threaten to damage the sails and rigging. In such conditions, there is not much the crew can do but secure what they can and pray that Manann decides to calm the seas. 

A successful **Challenging (+0) Boat Handling** Test must be made to take the sail down in time. If the Test is failed, the boat suffers an immediate Critical Hit to the sails as they are tossed about by the high winds. 

Whilst the winds continue to blow at this intensity, any vessel that is battened down must either deploy an Anchor or move at 25% of its normal speed in the direction the wind is blowing it. 

## **Navigation**
Finding and keeping your bearings is vitally important on the open ocean, where featureless horizons and unfamiliar coastlines can baffle even the most seasoned sailor. 

Like Tests for making forward progress, is it up to the GM to determine how often a Navigation Test needs to be made, but as a baseline, one Test should be made every day of travel. The results of the Navigation Test can then be compared to the Bearings table. 

||**BEARINGS**<br>**SL**<br>**Effects**<br>4 or<br>more<br>The Navigator knows which way the ship is<br>heading and, if they have access to the relevant<br>charts, can work out where the shipis on a map.<br>0 to 3<br>The ship is heading in the direction the<br>Navigator assumes it is heading.<br>–2 to –1<br>The ship is slightly of course. The discrepancy is<br>trivial, so this result has no effect the frst time,<br>but if the same result happens again, roll on the<br>Course Change table.<br>–3 to –4<br>The ship is of course. Roll on the<br>Course Change table.<br>–5 or<br>less<br>The ship is wildly of course. Roll on the Course<br>Change table and add 2 to the result.|
|---|---|

The Course Change table should be consulted every time something occurs that confuses the Navigator as to the direction of the ship. If the ship veers off course, the GM should roll d10 to see in what direction: 1–5 Starboard, 6–10 Port.

## **Lighthouses**
Lighthouses warn of hazards and assist navigation. Provided that they can see the light from a lighthouse, Characters with the Lore (Oceans) Skill may take a bonus to Navigation Tests equal to the first digit of their Skill score — so, a Character with a Lore (Oceans) Skill of 36 would receive a bonus of +3 to Navigation Tests. 

To perceive the light from a lighthouse, the Navigator must pass a Perception Test modified according to the following table (note that fog and mist may complicate matters, as explained under **Visibility** on page 106). 

## **Seeing the Light**
|**Distance to Lighthouse**|**Perception Test**<br>**to See Light**|
|---|---|
|Within 5 Miles|Easy (+40)|
|5–10 Miles|Challenging (+0)|
|10–15 Miles|Hard (–20)|

If the lighthouse is near a hazard, any Perception Tests made to spot that hazard benefit from +20. See page 112 for details of **Environmental Hazards at Sea** . 

## **Bell Towers**
Some ports, most famously Bilbali, use bell towers to guide ships rather than lighthouses. It is trickier to discern the direction from which the noise of the bell is coming, so bell towers only confer benefits of +2 SL to Navigation Tests. Sound normally dissipates sooner than light, so halve all the distances in the Seeing the Light Table for bell towers. However, they are beneficial in foggy weather, when the light from a lighthouse might be obscured. 

## **Chasing and Racing**
The rules for chasing and racing are adapted from those for pursuits on land. However, because the scale of such pursuits is so much larger at sea, running a pursuit using these rules may take a very long time. As such, we recommend that unless the crews of the boats involved in such pursuits are interacting in some other way (firing cannon at one another, casting spells, and so on) that Tests to determine Distance are made every ten Rounds, and the results multiplied by ten to find the actual Distance. 

If the results of the Tests indicate that the boats are now in a position where the crews may begin to interact with one another, then Tests to determine Distance should be taken every Round as normal. 

Should the crew of a boat wish to catch, escape, or otherwise outrun another vessel, some bookkeeping by the GM is required. Each boat involved in the race is treated as an individual. As with pursuits on land, the boat (or group of allied boats) being pursued are known as the Quarry, and those trying to catch them are known as the Pursuers. In a race, Pursuers who overtake the Quarry will become the Quarry themselves. 

**1: Determine Distance:** The GM assigns a number to represent the size of the head start the nearest member of the Quarry has over the closest Pursuer. This is the Distance.  Each point of Distance represents 10 yards. The Distance ranges from 0 (Quarry is caught) to a number the GM feels is appropriate for the Quarry to escape given the environment. The busier the environment, the smaller the number the Quarry must reach to escape. 

| Environment the Chase | Takes Place Within |
|---|---|
| **Distance Required** **to Escape** Tick fog banks, labyrinthine rock formations | 10 |
| Dim light, nearby fords or inlets | 30 |
| Light mist, many rocks and sandbanks in vicinity | 50 |
| Open water with a bit of chop | 70 |
| Still and open waters, clear day | 100 |

If the Quarry are in a tight group, they all count as being at the same Distance, but if any of them lead a Pursuer by more than 16 yards beyond another member of the Quarry, calculate their individual Distance from the Pursuers as appropriate. 

The Pursuers can be treated as a group if they have the same Movement, or split into smaller groups according to their Movement or ability to pass Tests to pursue. 

**2: Test and Update Distance:** In Initiative order, participants involved in the pursuit make Boat Handling Tests for their Movement, however, as it is less important to know how far the ship travels relative to other ships, use the table below rather than the one on page 104. 

Boats with M of 3 or less suffer penalties to Boat Handling Tests for pursuits. Boats with M 3 impose –1 SL, Boats with M 2 impose –2 SL, and Boats with M 1 impose –3 SL. 

**SL Effect** The boat moves forward the number of yards it would normally. Divide this number by 10, 4 or more rounding down to a minimum of 1. This number +1 is the Distance the boat moves this Round. The boat moves forward the number of yards it would normally. Divide this number by 0 to 3 10, rounding down to a minimum of 1 to determine Distance moved this Round. The boat moves forward the number of yards it would normally. Divide this number by 10, –1 to –3 rounding down to a minimum of 1. This number –1 is the Distance the boat moves this Round. The boat moves forward the number of yards it would normally. Divide this number by 10, –4 or less rounding down to a minimum of 1. This number –2 is the Distance the boat moves this Round. 

During this stage, if any Pursuer reduces the Distance to a member of the Quarry to 0 they can choose whether to engage them in fighting, or run past in the hope of catching a member of the Quarry further on. 

**3: Determine Outcome:** Recalculate the Distance between the various boats involved in the pursuit depending on their performance, then return to step 2. 

**Example:** A Norse longship is trying to catch up with an Imperial carrack. The longship has an M of 6 when using its oars, whilst the carrack has an M of 5 using its sails. 

The GM decides that the chase begins when the longship is outside of the range of the carrack’s guns. Because there is no meaningful way for the ships to interact other than alter their relative position, the GM decides that the tests made to pursue should be taken every 10 rounds, and their effects multiplied by ten until other interactions can take place. The GM decides that the initial distance between the vessels is 500 yards, and that the conditions are clear and upon the open ocean. He gives the carrack a head start of 50. 

The carrack is armed with a medium cannon facing towards the stern, with a range of 75 yards. The GM decides that if the longship reduces the distance to 21 then round by round tests will be made, as the carrack may then start targetting its pursuer with its cannon at extreme range. 

If the Carrack can increase the distance to 70, it escapes. The ships both make Boat Handling Tests, consulting the table on page 109 to determine their relative distances. 

Because these vessels both have large crews they may use Crew Tests (see page 121) in order to determine their success on Boat Handling Tests. 

The wind (see page 107) will also be a factor, as its direction and strength may affect the M of either vessel, but particularly the carrack. 

In this case the longship reduces the distance to 21, whereupon tests made for pursuit are made once a round. The carrack can now fire its cannon (and if the distance is reduced further other ranged weapons may play a part). 

The crew of the carrack had better hope that they can inflict enough damage on the longship to force it to abandon the pursuit before it reduces the distance to 0, or else a collision followed by a determined boarding action is sadly inevitable. 

## **Collisions**
Most of the time seafarers go to great pains to avoid collisions, but accidents happen, and on occasion a captain may order his vessel to ram another, as an attack or out of desperation. 

The Character or Characters who are best placed to serve as lookout have three chances to spot that another object is on a collision course with them. Once the hazard is spotted, the Character at the tiller must make a Manoeuvre Test to avoid it. The table below should give a rough guide, but the GM should bear in mind that hazards such as rocks below the waterline are harder to spot, whilst larger hazards are harder to avoid. 

||**HAZARD NEGOTIATION**<br>**Distance to**<br>**Hazard**<br>**Perception Test to Spot**<br>**Manoeuvre Test**<br>**to Avoid**<br>100yards<br>Hard(–20)<br>Easy (+40)<br>50 Yards<br>Challenging (+0)<br>Average(+20)<br>10 Yards<br>Average (+20)<br>Difcult (–10)|
|---|---|

Once it has passed, or collided with, the hazard, the ship will be off course. A Navigation Test should always be made after negotiating a hazard. 

## **Collision Ratings**
Vessels and many hazards have Collision Ratings. These vary according to how much mass and integrity the vessel or object possesses. For sake of simplicity the objects involved in the collision are referred to as boats, but they may be rocks, icebergs, sea monsters, and so on. 

A Collision Rating is worked out by adding the boat’s Toughness Bonus to its Wounds Bonus. So a boat with a Toughness of 20 and 15 remaining Wounds has a Collision Rating of 3. 

When one boat strikes another, each boat is hit for Damage equal to the other boat’s Collision Rating plus the M of the boat that caused the collision. 

## **Mitigating or Exacerbating Factors**
There are several factors that might make a collision more damaging, or less so. 

## **Mitigating or Exacerbating Factors**
|**Factor**|**Effect**|
|---|---|
|The boat receiving the collision is moving directly away from<br>the boat causingthe collision.|Reduce all Damage inficted by the M of the boat receiving<br>the collision.|
|Either boat is struck on the stern.|A boat struck on the stern benefts from 2 AP.|
|Either boat is struck amidships.|<br>Damage inficted to a boat struck amidships is doubled.|
|The boat causing the collision tries to manoeuvre in such a<br>way as to mitigate damage.|<br>The Character at the tiller of the ofending boat may make a<br>Manoeuvre Test. The number of SL generated is subtracted<br>from the Collision Ratingof both boats.|
|The boat causing the collision tries to manoeuvre in such a<br>way as to cause damage.|The Character at the tiller of the ofending boat may make a<br>Manoeuvre Test. The number of SL generated is added<br>to the Collision Ratingof both boats.|
|The boat receiving the collision tries to manoeuvre in such a<br>way as to mitigate damage.|The Character at the tiller of the receiving boat may make a<br>Manoeuvre Test. The number of SL generated is subtracted<br>from the Collision Ratingof both boats.|
|The boat receiving the collision tries to manoeuvre in such a<br>way as to cause damage.|The Character at the tiller of the receiving boat may make a<br>Manoeuvre Test. The number of SL generated is added<br>to the Collision Ratingof both boats.|
|Head-on collision.|Each boat is hit for Damage equal to the other boat’s<br>Collision Rating plus the total M of both boats involved.|

Unless otherwise specified, hits resulting from a collision always strike boats in the Hull location. 

## **Environmental Hazards at Sea**
The seas of the Old World are dangerous places, inhabited by monsters and crisscrossed by the raiding parties of hostile nations and species. There are also more prosaic hazards, such as those posed by the environment itself. 

## **Grounding**
Certain hazards may cause a boat to run aground. When a boat is grounded, it comes to a shuddering halt. The boat cannot move again until it is pulled free of the hazard. This task requires a Strength Test with a penalty equal to the total Encumbrance points of the boat and its cargo. Any number of Characters, draft animals, and so on can help, if there is enough rope for them all to pull on. 

## **Icebergs**
When a glacier meets the sea, chunks of packed ice and snow break off and form icebergs. Icebergs are pulled about by the wind or ocean currents and are often seen in the Sea of Claws and other cold oceans. 

An iceberg moves at a speed of M1. They vary greatly in mass, but an average iceberg has a Collision Rating of 25. 

## **Flotsam (or Jetsam)**
Debris from shipwrecks, lost cargo, or damaged trees drifts on the surface of the ocean. Whilst it is more of a nuisance than a danger, flotsam can prove to be trouble for smaller boats. 

Flotsam moves at a speed of M1. It has a Collision Rating of 3. If flotsam collides with a boat there is a 20% chance that it will become snagged. This imposes a penalty according to the size of the boat. 

- Boats of Size Tiny to Small: –2 SL to Man and –1 M. 

- Boats of Size Large: –1 SL to Man. 

## **Rocks and Shallows**
‘Rocks’ is a general term for any hard object that is fixed to the seabed but reaches either just above or just below the surface of the water. This includes coral reefs, the rocks of the Dragon’s Maw, the shells of gigantic, deceased sea creatures, and other hard objects that might damage a boat. 

They vary greatly in size and mass, but an average rock has a Collision Rating of 47. If a collision with a rock occurs, there is a 20% chance that the vessel will have become grounded. 

Shallows are embankments of smaller rocks, sand, or mud. They vary greatly in size and mass, but a typical area of shallows has a Collision Rating of 10. Upon colliding with the shallows, there is a 40% chance that the vessel will become grounded. 

## **Straits**
Straits are areas of strong current. Some straits need only be considered when the tides turn, others always exert force. 

Straits should be assigned an M value representing how strong and fast the current flows along them. 

The GM should decide before the boat encounters a strait which direction the current flows. A ship crossing a strait will be pulled in the direction of the current at the strait’s M before making any progress it would otherwise make. 

Whilst within a strait, all Boat Handling Tests are penalised as shown in the table below. 

||**BOAT HANDLING IN A STRAIT**<br>**Straight**<br>**M**<br>**Boat Handling Tests**<br>Weak<br>4<br>–1 SL<br>Average<br>8<br>–2 SL<br>Dire<br>16<br>–3 SL|
|---|---|

- Larger Boats: No effect. 

Crew may release snagged flotsam through an **Extended Average (+20) Strength** Test to a total of 10 SL. 

## **Whirlpools**
Whirlpools are bodies of rotating water caused by passing currents. Like straits, whirlpools have their own M values, representing the pull towards the centre. If a boat reaches the centre, it may not be able to escape, and the forces exerted by the rotating water may break the boat apart or drag it under. Whirlpools should be thought of as two different zones: the area (the body of water pulled towards the centre) and the centre (the middle of a whirlpool that may inflict damage on a vessel). Whirlpools have the following characteristics: 

**M:** This is the current, the rate by which objects caught in the area move towards the centre. 

If a ship enters the area, it moves towards the centre according to the whirlpool’s M each Round. The Character at the tiller must pass a Manoeuvre Test before the ship can proceed. If the ship can move beyond the area indicated by the first number, it escapes. Anyone swimming in the area must make a **Difficult (–10) Swim** Test or begin drowning. 

**Man:** Manoeuvre Tests within the area of the whirlpool are penalised as shown. 

**CR:** The Collision Rating at the centre of the whirlpool. Boats take Damage as if from a collision every Round unless they escape. 

**Area:** Area comprises two numbers: the first indicates how far in yards from the centre of the whirlpool it begins to exert a pull, and the second how far (in M, along a spiral path) an object travels from where it first feels the pull to where it reaches the centre of the whirlpool. 

**Escape:** The Test necessary to escape from the centre of the whirlpool. If the Character at the tiller passes this Test the boat may move away from the centre of the whirlpool. If this is enough to escape the whirlpool’s area, then the ship is safe. If not, it may be sucked towards the centre once again. 

## **Whirlpool Characteristics**
||**M**|**Area**|**Man**|**CR**|**Escape**|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Gentle<br>Rotation|2|15 yards/25|–|4|**Extended Average (+20) Manoeuvre**Test to a total of 10 SL|
|Whirlpool|4|30 yards/50|–1 SL|8|**Extended Challenging (+0) Manoeuvre**Test to a total of 20 SL|
|Powerful<br>Vortex|6|45 yards/75|–1 SL|12|**Extended Difcult (–10) Manoeuvre**Test to a total of 25 SL|
|A Maelstrom|8|60 yards/100|–2 SL|20|**Extended Hard (–20) Manoeuvre**Test to a total of 35 SL|
|_Te_Maelstrom|10|100 yards/150|–2 SL|50|**Extended Very Hard (–30) Manoeuvre**Test to a total of 45 SL|

**Example:** Being trapped in a whirlpool can be a tricky business. Here is discussion of the various factors that may play a part. Crew Tests are mentioned here but are covered in detail in Chapter 14. 

A carrack is caught on the edge of a whirlpool. This means it is at the far end of a spiral that is a total of 50 M from the edge of the whirlpool to the centre. 

The M of the whirlpool is 4 which is the distance the current will pull a stationary object towards the centre each round. 

The carrack has an M of 5 under sail. Because it is going round and round in the whirlpool, the GM rules that it will be affected by a tailwind on Round 1 and every subsequent odd numbered Round, then a headwind on Round 2 and every subsequent even numbered round. 

Each round, the boat is pulled 4 M around the area and towards the centre of the whirlpool. This movement occurs before any other movement is calculated. 

The Character at the tiller must pass a Manoeuvre test each turn before the ship can make any progress. The results of this test are modified by -1 SL. 

The Character at the tiller makes Boat Handling Tests to manoeuvre the vessel using their Sail Skill. Because the Carrack is a large vessel with many crew, they could combine their efforts to make a Crew Test to manoeuvre as explained on page 121.  In this circumstance, crew designated in any of the following roles — Captain, Navigator, Deckhand, _Helm_ , Chantyman — could make tests and combine their SL, with the Helm counting their SL twice. 

If the Manoeuvre Test is a success, the Character at the tiller may then make a Sail Test for making progress. They may benefit (or suffer from) factors such as the direction and strength of the wind (see page 107), and efforts to push it (see page 105). 

Because the Carrack is a large vessel with many crew, they could combine their efforts to make a Crew Test to make progress as explained on page 121.  In this circumstance, crew designated in any of the following roles — _Captain_ , Chantyman, Deckhand, Helm, Navigator — could make tests and combine their SL, with the Captain counting their SL twice. 

If the boat travels beyond the whirlpool’s area, it has no further problems, but if it is pulled into the centre of the whirlpool, it will start to take collision damage. 

The Collision Rating of the whirlpool is 8. This means that each Round, the Carrack will suffer a Damage 8 hit, meaning that it will suffer 3 Wounds after deducting its Toughness Bonus. With 90 wounds, it will take a long time for the whirlpool to break the Carrack apart, though such a fate is inevitable if it cannot escape the whirlpool. 

In order to do so, it must pass an **Extended Challenging (+0) Manoeuvre** T est to a total of 20 SL. The Character at the tiller makes Sail Tests in order to do so, but Crew Tests to manoeuvre may be taken instead. 

If the Test to Manoeuvre is passed, the Character at the tiller may then make a test for progress to see how far from the centre the boat travels. If it escapes the area of the whirlpool, it is safe. If not, it may be sucked back in. 

## **Damaging Boats**
Boats each have a Toughness score which modifies Damage taken, and a Wounds score which shows how much Damage they can take. 

To determine Hit Location, either reverse the score on the attack dice, as in Character combat (WFRP, page 159), or roll d100. Then consult the appropriate column of the **Boat Hit Location** chart. 

||**BOAT HIT LOCATION**<br>**d100**<br>**Roll**<br>**Rowing Boat**<br>**Sailing Boat**<br>**Boat with Oars**<br>**and Sails**<br>01–09<br>Crew<br>Crew<br>Crew<br>10–20<br>Oars<br>Rigging<br>Rigging<br>21–40<br>Hull<br>Hull<br>Oars<br>41–65<br>Hull<br>Hull<br>Hull<br>66–84<br>Fixtures<br>Fixtures<br>Fixtures<br>85–00<br>Cargo<br>Cargo<br>Cargo|
|---|---|

Crew hits indicate that an exposed crew member has been hit, and the results are determined as in normal combat. If no crew member is exposed, the blow strikes the hull. A crew hit on an open boat (such as a rowing boat) may hit the cargo rather than a crew member. 

## _Ablaze_ **Conditions**
_Ablaze_ Conditions affect a ship much like they do a character. A ship takes 1 Wound per turn per _Ablaze_ Condition. A single Ablaze Condition can only affect one location of the ship at a time. 

However, because ships are often made of wood, carry stores of explosives, or use flammable substances such as pitch to keep them watertight, a fire can quickly run out of control. To work out how bad the fire becomes, determine the initial intensity of the blaze: this is the number of _Ablaze_ Conditions in effect in any one location (other than the crew). At the end of each turn, roll on the **Fire Intensity** table to see if the fire spreads or intensifies. 

## **Fire Intensity**
|**d10**|**Effect**|**Notes**|
|---|---|---|
|1|Dies<br>Down|Roll d10 and subtract the result from<br>the intensity of the blaze. This is the<br>number of_Ablaze_Conditions to be<br>considered from the next turn onwards.|
|2–4|Steady<br>Burn|The intensity of the blaze is maintained.|
|5–8|Intense<br>Burn|Roll d10 and add the result to the<br>intensity of the blaze. This is the number<br>of_Ablaze_Conditions to be considered<br>from the next turn onwards.|
|9–10|Fire<br>Spreads|The intensity of the blaze is maintained,<br>but the fire also spreads to a second<br>location, breaking out there with d10<br>_Ablaze_Conditions. Roll on the Boat Hit<br>Location chart to determine the new<br>location. Any duplicate results,<br>or hits on the crew, are counted as<br>Intense Burn results instead.|

## **Small Arms Fire Against Ships**
Small arms fire, from ranged weapons other than artillery, generally does not do enough damage to trouble a ship. There is a chance that small arms fire aimed at the ship will still damage the crew, so it may be worth working out hits from small arms aimed at the ship in case they do strike an exposed crew member. 

It is up to the GM to decide whether NPCs firing small arms are aiming at individual crew members (which will often be difficult, as parts of the boat provide cover) or shooting at the boat (the ship will be a bigger target, but most shots will hit structures that ignore small arms fire — only a lucky few shots will strike crew members). Characters may make similar decisions for themselves. 

If a fire breaks out in the cargo bay, it can quickly ruin the goods. Each _Ablaze_ Condition renders d10 Enc worth of cargo ruined per turn, unless that cargo is somehow fireand smoke-proof. 

## **Melee Attacks Against Ships**
If enemies attack the crew directly, this is handled as an attack between characters. Any melee attack made against another part of the boat automatically hits, and Characters attacking a boat in melee may choose what location to attack, providing they can reach it. 

Melee weapons are not designed to damage boats, but it is possible to chip away at a vessel over time. A GM should note the size of the boat being attacked relative to the size of the attacking character. The TB of the boat is adjusted in the manner shown in the following table to account for the fact that most melee attacks struggle to inflict significant damage on a boat. If the result is blank, it means attacks from such characters will not normally inflict any damage to a boat. So if a Halfling (Size Small) attacks a Rowboat (Size Tiny) the boat will count its TB as triple when determining if it takes any damage. The same Halfling attacking a Large boat will not be able to inflict any damage. 

This comparison table replaces the normal modifiers for Damage that a Character might receive for being a certain Size, or relative Size to their opponent.

## **Repairing Boats**
Damage to a boat can be repaired permanently on a successful Trade (Boatbuilding) Test. Trade (Carpentry) can be used instead with a –10 penalty to all rolls. Suitable tools and materials, such as timber, pitch, canvas and so on, must be available. Damage to the Hull may only be repaired permanently if the boat is dragged onto a slipway or brought into a dry dock. 

A resident boat-builder can be found in most ports — an NPC Artisan with the Trade (Boat Building) Skill — who will repair boats for a fee of 1 GC per Wound restored. Each successful Test takes 1d10 hours of work and restores 1d10 Wounds to the boat. 

Some cultures have different traditions of boat building than others. Norse shipwrights, for example, are unfamiliar with the techniques required to build ships with forecastles and aftcastles, specialising instead in clinker-built hulls. They are unable to properly repair boats other than coracles, rowboats, knarrs, longships, and similar designs of vessel, though they could make temporary repairs to other craft. 

## **Temporary Repairs**
Temporary repairs may be made without dry-docking the boat. The **Trade (Boatbuilding)** or **Trade (Carpentry)** Test ranges from **Difficult (–10)** to **Very Hard (–30)** , depending on the working conditions. If the Test is successful, each repair takes one hour and restores 1d10 Wounds. 

However, the boat must make a Toughness Test for every full day of travel after temporary repairs are made. The boat must also take a Toughness Test whenever a Manoeuvre Test must be taken. Each failed Test results in 1d10–4 Damage as the temporary repair weakens. 

## **Boat Critical Hits**
When a double is rolled on a successful attack roll against a boat, it takes a Critical Hit. In addition, every hit after a boat’s Wounds score reaches zero is a Critical Hit. There are different designs of ship, and descriptions of Critical Hits may not apply to the vessel involved. In cases such as these, apply the next most serious Critical Hit. 

## **Critical Hits to the Crew**
Critical Wounds to crew are worked out according to the rules in **WFRP** (page 172) or **Up in Arms** (page 80). 

## **Critical Hits to the Ship**
When the ship takes a Critical Wound determine the location damaged, roll on the table for the location, and apply the effects. In addition to the listed effects, there may be further effects from particular types of damage. 

## **Splinters (Rating)**
During naval combat, many injuries are inflicted on the crew by cascades of splintered wood. If a Critical Hit results in Splinters, then a number of crew equal to the Rating are struck for 9 Damage. 

## **Holed (Rating)**
A Holed ship is taking on water. The GM should add the Rating to a running total that increases every Round. If this Rating reaches half the Toughness score of the boat, the vessel loses 1 M and gains a –1 SL penalty to all Boat Handling Tests as it sits heavily in the water. Unless the cargo is waterproof, it loses d10% of its value per turn until the hole is repaired and the hold bailed out. At this point, any gun ports must be closed or the Rating increases by 1. 

When the Rating equals the Toughness score of the boat, it sinks. 

Crew may try to mitigate the Rating by bailing out the water. Each member of the crew who devotes themself to bailing for ten Rounds may make a **Challenging (+0) Strength Test** . For every positive SL they generate on the Test, they may reduce the running total by 1. 

## **Falling from the Rigging**
Several Critical Hits may cause a Character to fall from the rigging. Consult the following table to determine how far they fall. Characters in the Crow’s Nest must also Test to see if they fall under such circumstances, and will fall even further than those in the rigging. 

||**FALLING FROM THE RIGGING**<br>**Boat Size**<br>**Fall from Rigging**<br>**Fall from Crow’s Nest**<br>**Tiny to**<br>**Small**<br>d10 yards<br>12 Yards<br>**Average to**<br>**Large**<br>2d10 yards<br>25 Yards<br>**Enormous to**<br>**Monstrous**<br>3d10 yards<br>40 Yards|
|---|---|

## **Repair**
The effects of Critical Wounds to a vessel can be mitigated by achieving the conditions listed. Suggested Extended Tests need only be taken if the repair is time-critical. If there is a competent member of the crew and suitable tools on board, it can be assumed that the repair takes place in a number of hours equal to the score in the d10 roll column of the Critical Wounds table (or the lowest of the numbers if a range is indicated).
